analysis.one_liner: Holds private equity funds liable for debts of firms they acquire and taxes fund managers' gains as ordinary income.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 10 Democratic cosponsors in October 2024, the bill was sent to four House committees, none of which ever held a hearing or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets private equity buyouts. It would make a private fund that takes control of a company legally responsible for that company's debts, legal penalties, and pension obligations; it would block the fund from paying itself big dividends, buybacks, or fee payments for four years after a takeover; and it would move workers' unpaid wages, severance, and benefits to the front of the line when a company goes bankrupt, while cutting off executive bonuses in bankruptcy. It also closes tax breaks for fund managers (including carried interest), restricts health care real estate deals that strip nursing homes and hospitals, extends fraud lookback windows for takeover-related transfers, and bars federal health programs from paying providers that sell their buildings to health care REITs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies owned by private equity funds, who keep their place in line for owed wages, severance, and benefits in bankruptcy and whose jobs weigh in court when a bankrupt company is sold. Retirees and pension beneficiaries gain because funds must absorb pension debts instead of passing them on. Taxpayers gain from closing the carried interest and related tax breaks. Nursing home residents, gift card holders, and striking workers also get specific protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at private-equity-owned companies and retirees

how_it_helps.text: Makes a controlling private equity fund, and its holders of active interests, jointly and severally liable for the acquired company's debts, fines, WARN Act violations, pension withdrawal liability, and Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation claims [S2].

Bars the acquired company from most capital distributions for four years after a takeover and caps later payouts, voiding transfers that break these limits and giving workers and creditors a court action to claw them back with attorney's fees [S2].

Raises bankruptcy priority for unpaid wages to $20,000 per worker, adds severance pay and welfare-benefit contributions to priority claims, and makes back pay and labor-law penalties payable as administrative expenses [S2].

Restricts executive bonuses and retention pay in bankruptcy, ties bankruptcy-court approval of executive compensation to what the nonmanagement workforce receives, and requires courts weighing a company sale to favor bids that preserve jobs and employment terms [S2].

Treats investment fund managers' carried-interest gains as ordinary income rather than lower-taxed capital gains, limits interest deductions for private-fund-owned firms, and imposes a surtax on payments from portfolio companies to controlling investment firms [S2].

Cuts off Medicare and Medicaid payments to health care providers that sell assets to, or pledge them as collateral with, a real estate investment trust, and repeals related tax preferences for health care REIT subsidiaries [S2].

Extends the bankruptcy lookback for fraudulent transfers connected to a change-of-control deal to 15 years, narrows the safe harbor that has protected such transfers, and makes it an unfair labor practice to permanently replace strikers or lock out workers to influence bargaining [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds and their general partners bear the core costs: full liability for portfolio company debts and pension shortfalls, a four-year freeze on post-takeover payouts, and a surtax on money extracted from controlled firms. Fund managers pay through the end of the carried interest tax preference and stricter disclosure and fiduciary rules. Health care REITs lose federal health program revenue from sale-leaseback arrangements, and private credit lenders and securitizers face risk-retention and transparency requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity funds, fund managers, health care REITs

drawbacks.text: Joint and several liability for every debt of an acquired company, including acquisition loans, goes far beyond a fund's actual investment and could raise the cost of buyout financing, reduce capital available to struggling companies, or push deals into structures the bill does not reach [S2].

The four-year ban on capital distributions applies even to legitimate returns owed to pension funds and endowments that invest in private equity, and the bill's own definitions exempt pension funds from liability while their returns still depend on distributions [S2].

Section 209 rewrites broad sections of the National Labor Relations Act governing striker replacement and bargaining, so a bill billed as anti-looting would change labor law well beyond the private equity context [S2].

Banning Medicare and Medicaid payments to any provider that sells property to a REIT could cut off refinancing capital that some nursing homes and hospitals use to stay open, with the burden falling on facilities in weak financial condition [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker, retiree, and taxpayer protections respond to real and well-documented harms: the bill's own findings list retailers like Sears and Toys \"R\" Us and vulnerable sectors like nursing homes that were loaded with debt and stripped after buyouts [S2]. The costs fall almost entirely on the private equity industry and its investors, which is the bill's stated purpose. The honest tradeoffs are the breadth of the joint liability rule, which could chill legitimate investment, and the sweeping labor-law rider, which expands the bill beyond its core subject.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to four House committees the day it was introduced; none of them acted, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the Stop Wall Street Looting Act on October 11, 2024, with nine original cosponsors, late in the second session of the 118th Congress [S1] [S2].
The bill was referred the same day to four committees — Ways and Means, Financial Services, Judiciary, and Education and the Workforce — splitting it among panels with overlapping jurisdiction [S4].
It gained one additional cosponsor for a total of 10, all House Democrats [S3].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the initial referral, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity funds and their managers are better off because the bill died: they remain shielded from portfolio company debts, keep the four-year-free dividend and buyback playbook, keep the carried interest tax preference, and health care REITs keep collecting federal health program money from sale-leaseback deals.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity funds and their managers

sides.party_line_note: All 11 supporters — the sponsor and 10 cosponsors — were House Democrats, no Republican cosponsored, and no committee chaired by either party advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill strikes at the core buyout model: a fund that takes control of a company would be on the hook for its debts, pension obligations, and legal penalties, and could not strip the company through dividends and buybacks for four years. These rules exist because fund gains from debt-loaded takeovers have repeatedly come at the expense of workers and communities, as the bill's own findings catalog [S2].

industries.industry: Hedge fund and buyout fund managers
industries.note: Fund managers would pay ordinary income tax rates on carried interest gains instead of capital gains rates, face a surtax on payments extracted from controlled companies, and owe fiduciary duties and fee-and-return disclosures to investors. The tax preference they would lose is a direct federal subsidy to the wealthiest fund managers.

Any provider that sells its buildings to a REIT or pledges them as REIT collateral would lose Medicare and Medicaid payments, and tax preferences for health care REIT subsidiaries would be repealed. This targets the sale-leaseback structure in which REITs collect rent from nursing homes and hospitals that still depend on federal health dollars.

industries.industry: Private credit lenders and corporate debt securitizers
industries.note: The bill imposes risk-retention requirements on securitized corporate debt and requires visibility into non-bank direct lending and private credit, so lenders and securitizers would have to keep a stake in the risk they currently pass to investors.

industries.industry: Pension funds and endowments as private fund investors
industries.note: Pension funds are expressly shielded from control-person liability, but as investors they would face funds that cannot pay out returns for four years after a takeover and must disclose fees, returns, and performance honestly. Many public-employee pensions are invested in these funds, so stronger rules could cut both ways for their beneficiaries.
